title: Meet the operating system
subtitle: Your first five minutes inside the machine
production: AI-authored script and diagrams, locally rendered with synthetic narration. These are teaching illustrations, not live Windows recordings.
summary: Discover programs, processes, threads, private virtual addresses, and the boundary between application work and Windows services. Then investigate a healthy workstation using evidence.

sources.label: Microsoft: user mode and kernel mode

chapters.title: Welcome to the training workstation
chapters.takeaway: Your mission: understand the mechanism, not memorize the label.
narration: Welcome to Inside the Machine, where a training workstation lets you experiment, make predictions, and discover what happens behind an application.
Level one starts with an installed program and a running instance; no debugger, Windows experience, or virtual machine is needed.
Your goal is to connect a few observations into a useful explanation of a healthy application, rather than memorize disconnected names.

chapters.title: A program can exist without running
chapters.takeaway: Installed is not the same as executing.
narration: Atlas Notes is installed but not open: its executable is a program on disk, containing instructions and data that can be loaded.
The file remains when no instances are running, so finding it in a folder does not prove that instructions are executing.
In First Contact, inspect the file, predict what launching changes, and watch the process list: installed is not the same as running.

chapters.title: One program, independent processes
chapters.takeaway: Separate running instances can share an executable, not an identity.
narration: Our fictional Atlas Notes supports independent instances: opening it twice creates two processes from one executable, each with a different live process identifier.
Close one and observe the survivor; the executable remains, because closing an instance does not uninstall the program.
Real applications may reuse or create multiple processes; this model is deliberately simple, and Windows can reuse identifiers after a process exits.

chapters.title: A process holds context and resources
chapters.takeaway: A process is more than a window.
narration: A process holds execution context and resources, including a virtual address space and one or more threads that can execute instructions.
It is more than a window: processes can exist without visible windows, and a visible application can involve several processes.
For now, inspect identity and ownership: which process owns this work, what belongs to it, and what does your evidence actually establish?

chapters.title: Threads do the executing
chapters.takeaway: Windows schedules threads, not an entire process as one unit.
narration: Threads execute instructions inside a process: one might handle interface work while another performs an export, both belonging to the same process.
A long export on the interface thread can delay input; moving suitable work to a worker can help the interface progress.
But another thread does not create more processor capacity; distinguish who owns the work from when it can actually run.

chapters.title: Taking turns is not running in parallel
chapters.takeaway: More threads do not automatically mean simultaneous execution.
narration: On one logical processor, our model runs one thread at a time; multiple threads can make progress by taking turns.
A ready thread can run; a waiting thread needs an event or resource first, so unfinished work does not necessarily mean busy computation.
This timeline illustrates states, not Windows scheduling policy; later levels explore processors and dependencies, while today you distinguish ready, running, and waiting.

chapters.title: An address needs a process context
chapters.takeaway: The same virtual address need not refer to the same data.
narration: A virtual address needs an address-space context: the same written address in two processes need not refer to the same underlying data.
In A Private Address Book, inspect separate mappings, change one process's value, and read the other value to check your prediction.
Do not confuse the virtual map with physical memory; deeper questions about backing, commitment, and residency belong to the memory level.

chapters.title: Isolation is a model, not a magical wall
chapters.takeaway: This experiment uses separate mappings; sharing is possible.
narration: Separate address spaces help isolate ordinary application memory, but processes can still communicate or intentionally share memory through suitable mechanisms.
Our experiment excludes shared mappings and cross-process access, so an unchanged second value describes these particular mappings, not every possible interaction.
Explain the experiment's conditions as well as its result; later, sharing and copy-on-write will add depth to this address-space model.

chapters.title: Follow a request across the boundary
chapters.takeaway: A service request does not require a new process.
narration: Applications can calculate in user mode, while selected operations, such as our modeled file request, need services across the user and kernel boundary.
Follow the request: in this service path, the same calling thread enters kernel mode and returns with a result, without creating another process.
Not every application interface enters the kernel, and kernel mode does not guarantee unrestricted access; permissions still matter.

chapters.title: Build a map of responsibilities
chapters.takeaway: A conceptual map explains cooperation, not a universal call stack.
narration: Connect the pieces: applications request services, executive components manage memory and input and output, and the kernel coordinates activities including thread scheduling.
Drivers participate in selected device paths, with hardware underneath; explain these responsibilities using the request traces you have already followed.
This maps cooperation, not a universal call sequence; also distinguish the kernel component from everything that executes in kernel mode.

chapters.title: Predict, experiment, explain, transfer
chapters.takeaway: A wrong prediction is useful; an unsupported explanation is not mastery.
narration: Predict, change a small model, and inspect evidence: a mistaken prediction opens a learning opportunity rather than costing points.
Choose observations that support your explanation, use hints if needed, and apply the concept to a changed situation rather than repeat buttons.
This video is optional; investigations unlock mastery without a timer, while deeper notes and references remain available when you want more detail.

chapters.title: Your Level 1 mission
labels: Follow and justify an OS request
chapters.takeaway: Start First Contact. Small discoveries become a connected mental model.
narration: By the end, distinguish a program, a process, and a thread using observations, not definitions alone, and explain why a virtual address needs context.
Follow a selected operating-system request and connect the ideas into an evidence-backed description of a healthy workstation.
This is a teaching campaign, not live Windows telemetry or a complete emulator; start First Contact when ready, and build understanding one discovery at a time.
